fields.question: Why define FLINT padding masks and fully masked inputs explicitly?
fields.answer: Padding cannot participate in cross-attention; local True denotes valid tokens and wholly masked rows fail. Preserve pre-LN and both residual stages, not a bare attention pool.
fields.example: Padding half a batch must not change what latents read.

fields.question: Why calibrate on the deployed 1.5 approximation to √2 in FPoT?
fields.answer: Exact half-exponent calibration followed by approximate execution adds unoptimized error. Choose scale and phase for the real shift-add grid. Integer shifts round, and activation/KV formats are separate.
fields.example: A code calibrated at √2×scale runs at 1.5×scale; awareness lets calibration choose a better code or scale.

fields.question: Why insert half octaves in a power-of-two grid?
fields.answer: Half-exponent spacing increases four-bit resolution, while odd exponents use 1.5 for shift-add. This trades accuracy and execution rather than allowing arbitrary floating values.
fields.example: A level near 1.5 is finer than only one or two.

fields.question: Do FPoT weights, activations, and KV use one format?
fields.answer: No. Weights use a half-octave grid; activations and KV use uniform integers. Account for each format and execution cost separately.
fields.example: Shift-add weight codes do not remove activation scaling rules.

fields.question: Why subtract one from nonzero magnitude code m?
fields.answer: Zero has a reserved code and m=e+1 otherwise. Recover e=m−1 for parity and shift. Signed right shifts can round, so do not claim exact real multiplication by 1.5.
fields.example: Magnitude code one is e=0, not an odd exponent.

fields.question: Does GQA reduce Q heads or KV heads, and why does it save decode memory?
fields.answer: Many query heads share fewer K/V heads while retaining different queries. Each historical position stores and reads fewer KV groups. This reduces independence compared with MHA, not history token count.
fields.example: Eight queries can use two KV groups while producing eight different attention distributions.

fields.question: Why share fewer K/V heads among more queries?
fields.answer: Queries keep distinct directions while grouped history lowers cache and read bandwidth. It interpolates between per-head MHA and single-group MQA.
fields.example: Four query heads can share two stored KV histories instead of four.

fields.question: Which head-count axis distinguishes MHA, GQA, and MQA?
fields.answer: MHA generally has one KV per Q, GQA shares within groups, and MQA shares globally. Query head count can remain fixed; quality and bandwidth are empirical.
fields.example: Keep eight Q heads with eight, two, or one KV group.

fields.question: Does temporarily expanding shared KV establish cache savings?
fields.answer: No. Logical broadcast can aid compute, but persistent KV must store fewer groups; retaining expanded copies loses savings. Check g(h) and distinguish local from original uptraining.
fields.example: Four Q heads sharing two groups should store two histories.

fields.question: Why retain projection bases for one IrekoGPT checkpoint to support nested widths?
fields.answer: Dropping directions fixes width. Ordered bases let each width take a prefix, and multi-ratio calibration and linear correction reduce error. Shared structure does not equal shared quality or measured throughput.
fields.example: Switch between narrow and wide subnets only if extra basis directions were not discarded.

fields.question: Why expose nested widths from one checkpoint?
fields.answer: One ordered basis supports several budget levels without separately stored pruned models. Width k takes its first k directions and receives calibration.
fields.example: Narrow and wide paths share the same ordered basis.

fields.question: How do nested widths differ from single-ratio pruning in deployment?
fields.answer: Single-ratio pruning retains one width. Nested storage and calibration allow runtime k selection, but do not guarantee every width's quality or speed.
fields.example: Validating k=64 does not validate k=32 automatically.

fields.question: Why not fit an independent projection basis per width?
fields.answer: W_k=P_:kᵀWP_:k requires prefixes of one basis. Independent choices break nesting. Preserve downstream linear calibration and ridge correction; local scope is subnet diagnosis.
fields.example: The 32-wide basis must be the first 32 directions of the 64-wide basis.

fields.question: Why doesn't separating KVMEM's address space from execution window mean all-history attention?
fields.answer: Store paged KV across tiers, retrieve relevant blocks in attention space, and materialize a bounded native-window view. Missed evidence stays out. Local full backing cache and no complete async tiering mean no VRAM or speed claim.
fields.example: Load a few old KV pages per query, not every page at once.

fields.question: Why page long agent histories as KV?
fields.answer: History can exceed memory and context; summaries may lose details. KVMEM stores computed KV in tiers, indexes relevant blocks, and materializes a native-window view.
fields.example: Many pages can exist while only several are loaded per execution.

fields.question: How does paged KV reuse differ from retrieving text and prefilling it?
fields.answer: Paged reuse materializes computed K/V; text retrieval usually computes K/V again. Position, storage, and consistency contracts differ, so retrieval count alone is not cost.
fields.example: Fetch cached KV versus fetch tokens and calculate their KV anew.

fields.question: Why not claim lower peak VRAM while retaining full backing cache?
fields.answer: A bounded working set does not prove offload. Local Python retains backing cache and does not establish production kernels. Report working set, residency, movement, and end-to-end time separately.
fields.example: Reading 512 of 2048 resident slots still occupies all 2048.

fields.question: Why buffer high-precision updates in a window instead of quantizing each step?
fields.answer: Repeated rounding feeds back into recurrence. Keep a low-bit base plus precise increments and requantize at boundaries; separate compensation protects outlier directions. Buffer and compensation cost memory. Local truncated SVD is not the original kernel or throughput.
fields.example: Accumulate tiny updates before rounding so each is not lost individually.

fields.question: Why address both repeated rounding and state outliers?
fields.answer: Recurrence accumulates quantization error and outliers dominate scale. Window buffering reduces rounding frequency; high-precision compensation separates large directions before residual quantization.
fields.example: Do not recompress every token or let one direction consume the entire grid.

fields.question: What is the trade-off between window buffers and low-bit writes every step?
fields.answer: Buffers add temporary high-precision state but reduce whole-state requantization; stepwise writes round more often. Count base, updates, and compensation.
fields.example: Buffering eight updates before one quantization differs from eight whole-state writes.

fields.question: Should the low-bit part quantize S or S−C?
fields.answer: Form C from truncated SVD, quantize S−C, then add C at readout. Quantizing full S and adding C counts it twice. Merge precise window updates at the prescribed boundaries.
fields.example: An outlier direction stored in C need not be stored in full in the residual too.

fields.question: Why reserve routing anchors in a normal MoE KV compression budget?
fields.answer: KV deletions can change attention and subsequent routing. Propagate Fisher sensitivity from observed instruction positions through attention, reserve anchors, then fill with the base compressor. Sensitivity is a proxy, not a route-flip guarantee or permission to read gold.
fields.example: An older low-attention token can still affect expert choice and merit retention.

fields.question: Why connect KV error to MoE routing?
fields.answer: Eviction perturbs attention outputs seen by the router. Attention quality alone can miss route-sensitive positions, so estimate anchors from observed instruction gates and attention.
fields.example: A nonmaximal KV can move a token across an expert boundary.

fields.question: Is Fisher trace an exact top-k router flip criterion?
fields.answer: No. It averages distribution curvature over directions and omits the router-to-hidden Jacobian. High trace does not imply a flip.
fields.example: Equal trace at two positions can yield different routing changes under different perturbation directions.

fields.question: Can the base compressor select anchors again when filling budget?
fields.answer: No. Exclude already selected anchors and fill with distinct positions. Gather real KV in original temporal order. Use prefill instruction only, never future gold diagnostics.
fields.example: With 64 slots and 16 anchors, add 48 distinct non-anchor positions.
